x: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and cutting the blood's oxygen supply.
t: Recall how CO harms the blood.

x: Option C is incorrect: burning fuel is a human-made (anthropogenic) source. Volcanoes and forest fires are natural sources.
t: Sort sources into natural and human-made.

x: Both are true: photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons react in sunlight, which is why it is linked with all three. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the ingredients explain the link.

x: CO comes from vehicle exhaust, SO₂ from burning fossil fuels and causes acid rain, lead from leaded petrol, and fly ash from thermal power plants. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Match each pollutant to its source.

x: All four are correct: smog is smoke plus fog, WAYU devices clean traffic air, Oilzapper bacteria clean oil spills, and CNG is mainly methane.
t: Match each term to its link.

x: All three are correct: industries pollute the air, and both nitrogen oxides and PM2.5/PM10 come from combustion and vehicles.
t: Match each pollutant to its source.

x: Carbon monoxide is singled out as a dangerous air pollutant because it is colourless and odourless and blocks oxygen transport in the blood.
t: Recall why CO is dangerous.

x: Lichens are indicators of air pollution because they die when SO₂ is high. Decibels measure noise.
t: Recall the bio-indicator of air quality.

x: Both are true: nitrogen oxides pollute the air, and they cause acid rain. Acid rain is one effect, not why NOx counts as an air pollutant, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether one effect explains the general claim.

x: PAN is peroxyacyl nitrate, a part of photochemical smog; a green muffler (a belt of trees) cuts noise, and noise is measured in decibels. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each term to its link.

x: Both are true: rustling leaves make about 20 dB and a rocket engine about 180 dB.
t: Recall the noise levels.

x: All four are correct: fertilisers pollute soil, water and air, and their nitrates and phosphates cause eutrophication of water bodies.
t: Recall the effects of fertiliser.

x: The Water Act dates from 1974 and the Water Cess Act from 1977; arsenic pollution is linked with Kolkata (West Bengal), and UV light kills microbes in water. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Match each item to its detail.

x: On the AQI, 401–500 is 'Severe'. 301–400 is Very Poor, 201–300 Poor, and 101–200 Moderate.
t: Recall the AQI bands.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, was amended in 1987, not 1991.
t: Recall the Air Act amendment year.

x: SO₂ comes from fuel burning, power stations, industry and diesel, CO from transport, O₃ forms in the air by photochemical reactions, and benzene comes from petrol. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Match each pollutant to its source.

x: I, II and III are correct: NCAP began in January 2019, aiming to cut PM10 and PM2.5 by 20–30% by 2024 from 2017 levels. IV is false because 1981 is the Air Act.
t: Discriminate NCAP from the Air Act.

x: Particulate matter is PM10, fine particulate matter PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide NO₂, and carbon monoxide CO. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match each pollutant to its symbol.

x: Ozone is O₃, sulphur dioxide SO₂, ammonia NH₃, and lead Pb. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each pollutant to its symbol.

x: All five are correct: 0–50 is Good, 51–100 Satisfactory, 101–200 Moderate, 201–300 Poor, and 301–400 Very Poor.
t: Recall the AQI bands.

x: All five are major sources of PM10 and PM2.5: construction, combustion, diesel exhaust, road dust, and biomass and household burning.
t: Recall the sources of particulate matter.

x: Both are true: fuel burning and industry are both major sources of PAH. Naming a second source does not explain the first, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a second source explains the first.

x: Solvents, industry and households are VOC sources, while fuel, industrial and soil particles are lead sources. The answer is a-i, b-i, c-i, d-ii, e-ii, f-ii.
t: Allow codes to repeat.

x: Both are true: NCAP takes a broad approach to air pollution, and it began in January 2019. Its launch date does not explain its approach, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a date explains an approach.

x: The CPCB was set up in September 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and later given air duties under the Air Act, 1981.
t: Recall the CPCB's parent Act.

x: Option C is incorrect: the CPCB works at the national level. State Pollution Control Boards handle the State level.
t: Discriminate the CPCB from the SPCBs.

x: Both are true: the Water Act aims to prevent and control water pollution so that water stays wholesome. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the aim explains the purpose.

x: The CPCB works at the central level, SPCBs at State level, the Water Act prevents and controls water pollution, and the boards monitor water bodies and industrial discharges. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each body to its role.

x: Both are true: SPCBs carry out pollution control in the States, and the boards can act against violators.
t: Recall the powers of the pollution boards.

x: The CPCB deals with water pollution (under the 1974 Act) and air pollution (under the 1981 Act).
t: Recall the CPCB's two Acts.
